title: Interoperability and Data Exchange
keywords: integrating numpy with the python ecosystem
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of interoperability and data exchange and name one situation where it is useful.
Apply buffer protocol concepts to a small NumPy example and inspect the resulting values, shape, or dtype.
Identify one important limitation, boundary case, or validation check for interoperability and data exchange.

content.intro: This lesson develops topic 200 of the supplied curriculum: **Interoperability and Data Exchange**. The main starting point is **Buffer protocol concepts**. You will connect the idea to a small, synthetic example, then use the result to reason about shape, dtype, accuracy, or memory as appropriate.
content.why_it_matters: Scientific Python tools share ndarray data, but each library has its own contract. Check shape, dtype, mutability, missing values, and conversion/copy behavior at boundaries.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Treat **Interoperability and Data Exchange** as an explicit step in an array workflow. This lesson centers on **Buffer protocol concepts** and the source syllabus's related subtopics. Before trusting a result, identify the input shape and dtype, perform the smallest useful operation, and inspect the output. The example uses synthetic data so you can change one value and observe what changes.

content_blocks.code:
import numpy as np

arr = np.frombuffer(bytes([1, 2, 3, 4]), dtype=np.uint8)
print(arr.tolist())

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a downstream library never copies or converts
common_mistakes.why: Boundary adapters can coerce dtype or allocate new arrays.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the receiving library's documented conversion and mutability behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a NumPy array as a generic tensor everywhere
common_mistakes.why: Array libraries can differ in device, dtype, and operation semantics.
common_mistakes.fix: Document conversions and validate shapes and types at the boundary.
